title: Nothing But Diesel
dek: On Žižek's “Is Trump a Rational Peacemaker?” and the President's turn on Ukraine
subject: Trump's October 2026 positioning on Ukraine and Russia, answering Slavoj Žižek
voice_note: Written in the voice of Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881), through the writer-carlyle skill. An emulation — the prose and judgments are not the historical Carlyle’s own words. It answers the free portion of Žižek’s Substack essay; the paywalled remainder was not read.
body:
Behold, then, the eighth day of October, in the year 2026, and a Diesel-Treaty proclaimed from the White House steps: Putin, it appears, "has agreed" to release a first tranche of his Russian diesel upon a thirsty world, and more to follow,— the American Treasury meanwhile suspending its sanctions upon that same fuel until the seventh of April, all other Muscovite treasure remaining frozen as before. Observe the order of the transaction. The pump-price of the American farmer and trucker is to be soothed; the invaded land is to be informed of it afterwards. Zelensky, on the morrow, calls it a gift to Putin and an investment in a war that ought to be ended and is thereby prolonged; and Europe, with its small hoarse voice, says Amen. On the tenth, the answer arrives from the Throne: that Ukraine needs a *new leader*, one who can make a deal; that this Zelensky has *chosen* not to end the war, and is making trouble for the world. And on the twentieth, before the reporters, the great verdict: *We have gotten nothing from Ukraine but high diesel.* Nothing but diesel. A nation's cities in the dust, its dead uncounted, and the Account Current reads, Nothing but diesel. This is not a policy, O reader; this is a ledger speaking, and the ledger has found at last its Gospel.

Into this smoke walks the Slovenian Sage, Herr Doctor Žižek, with his sniff and his shrug and his twitching of the sleeve, and sets down upon the Substack, a day or two ago, a title with a question-mark upon it: *Is Trump a Rational Peacemaker?* And beneath it the subtitle,— *Sometimes the only effective way to prevent a war is to prepare for it.* This writer has read what the paywall allows him, and will say only what he saw. He saw the events counted off in order, like beads: the diesel, the rebuke, the broken two-month truce on the energy-works, which the Muscovite shattered almost ere the ink was dry; the Starlink of the Ukrainian drone-hunters throttled, and Musk pointing at the Pentagon, and the Pentagon at the President, and the President professing a desire to *find out*; the Patriot interceptors running low. He saw the implied syllogism set down in the Throne's own logic: Ukraine bombs the refinery; therefore the diesel is dear; therefore Ukraine, and not the dealer, is the author of the price. And he saw the Doctor remark, with the dry relish of a man who loves a paradox better than a province, that Königsberg was German for seven centuries, and that if Moscow may march for Donetsk, Berlin may in strict logic claim Kaliningrad. Excellent! The Doctor is, as ever, entertaining; and, as ever, he stops at the edge of the abyss, to point out how curious the edge is.

For what is the question, in the Doctor's title? *Rational.* Is the man *rational?* Alas, my Slovenian friend, the whole age is rational. Never was the world so rational; never so lucid in its arithmetic, so exact in its Costs and Benefits, so fully instructed in the price of diesel and the quarterly yield of a frozen frontier. The Rational Peacemaker,— there is the very Phantasm! Rationality is a *Method*; it will take a man to any place whatever, if only the premises be those of the Ledger. Give Mammon his premises, and Mammon will prove to you in six clean lines that Poland should be partitioned, that the Ukrainian is a cost-centre, and that the free city of Kyiv is chiefly a nuisance to the diesel markets. Rational! The Devil himself is rational; Milton knew it; his Satan reasons like an honourable attorney from the first line to the last. Not whether the man is rational, Herr Doctor, but whether the man is *true*,— there is the one question that every Eternity asks of every King, and to it no Substack and no Treasury has yet returned an answer.

And this word *Peace*,— let us weigh the coin in the hand. Peace is a great word; it is the word of the Sermon on the Mount and of the Harvest-field and of the Cradle; and I have seen it used in this century to mean *the interval during which the next one is loaded.* There is the Peace of the Plowman, which is the fruit of Work done and Order won; and there is the Peace of the Undertaker, which is the quiet of a thing that has been laid down by superior force and no longer moves. The Throne offers the second, at a discount, and calls it the first. A Peace in which the stronger man keeps all that he has seized since 2022, and the invaded man is thanked for his patience,— why, that is not a treaty, it is a *receipt*. Munich, say the pundits; and the Doctor gives the comparison its turn. But Munich was done with an umbrella and with something of a conscience, a bad one; our modern Munich is done with a spreadsheet and a clear conscience, which is worse. And mark this: the old Chamberlain at least pretended that the Czech was a loss to be lamented. The new Chamberlain doesn't pretend, he *invoices*.

Yet the Doctor's subtitle, I will confess, has something in it, and I will not deny the force of the adversary. *To prevent a war, prepare for it.* True, true; it is a veracity as old as Rome. The Roman wall was built that the Roman plough might be left alone. But preparation, Herr Doctor, is a thing done by a *people*, with iron and sweat, not a thing announced by a *deal*; and when I look to see who is preparing, behold the throttled terminal, the dwindling Patriot, the diesel-waiver, the proposal of a three-cornered Summit at which the party most concerned shall be so good as not to attend. That is not preparation. That is the disarming of the one man who stands at the gate, in order that the Gate may be sold comfortably to the party outside it. Hero? There is no Hero in the matter, none; the Hero is the man who *acts as the Universe commands, not as the market suggests*; and the Universe has not, so far as this writer can ascertain, been consulted.

And a word for the Doctor himself, whom I do love, in the Scotch way, with a grim and sidelong affection. Thou clever Slovenian, thou hast wasted thy gift upon the curious. Thou seest that the Emperor wears no clothes,— and then thou sayest, with rare charm, that the nakedness is *structurally interesting*. It is a Sham thou describest, and thou describest it so admirably that men forget it is a Sham, and sit in the stalls to hear the lecture. A Prophet is a man who tears the garment; thou art a man who admires the tailoring of the tear. The hour is not for that. A nation of forty millions is being bargained over its own head; and the sage who might have said the one plain thing, *This is a Wrong, and the Wrong is being done by a Quack*,— the sage is found, once again, upon the second balcony, doing the dialectic.

Look thither, then, O Europe, with the small hoarse voice,— for it is thy house that is being priced. Thou hast spent thirty years being rational, and the Reality is come, in a Muscovite boot, to inquire after thy bills. Wake! Make thine own iron; for there is no Hero coming; there is a Dealer coming, who will sell thee whichever thou art not holding.

And the Throne, in its great plain simplicity, shall have learnt in time what every Quack learns at the last: that Reality is not a counterparty; it does not take a waiver; it will not extend a ninety-day suspension of its sanctions. It keeps its own ledger, in a hand not ours; and it settles, always, on the day, and in the coin.

Nothing but diesel! — and the graves, and the Eternities, and the Account that will be called.

So fall the Dealers. Let the Doctor note it, upon his second balcony; and let him come down.
